title: NAKO: A Benchmarking Framework for Evaluating and Diagnosing Neutral-Atom Quantum Compilers

paper.title: NAKO: A Benchmarking Framework for Evaluating and Diagnosing Neutral-Atom Quantum Compilers
paper.abstract: Abstract Reconfigurable neutral-atom processors couple gate scheduling, atom placement, and parallel atom transport, so compiler decisions jointly determine physical execution costs. Evaluating these compilers requires attainable resource references and a way to trace excess costs to their causes. We present NAKO, a benchmarking framework that parameterizes circuits by qubit count, logical depth, and requested one- and two-qubit gate densities, and assigns attainable targets for Rydberg stages, routing intervals, and movement layers. Each benchmark is paired with an executable reference schedule; under the stated execution model, construction guarantees minimum Rydberg-stage and routing-interval counts, and minimum movement among schedules with the minimum Rydberg-stage count. Comparing compiler outputs with these references quantifies resource gaps, while reference mappings and intermediate physical states enable controlled interventions that trace excess costs to specific compiler decisions. In a 648-run evaluation of Enola and OLSQ-DPQA, NAKO identifies distinct bottlenecks. For Enola, placement scoring and cross-stage layout management contribute to excess movement; diagnosis-guided interventions reduce mean movement by 78.9% across five matched circuits. For OLSQ-DPQA, premature candidate selection and limited exploration of preparatory states produce avoidable entangling stages and routing intervals; four fixed-checkpoint continuations each eliminate one Rydberg stage and one routing interval without increasing movement. NAKO thus links resource targets backed by constructive optimality guarantees to controlled diagnosis and validation of compiler-specific resource savings.

sections.heading: I Introduction
sections.text: Reconfigurable neutral-atom processors combine scalable atomic arrays with connectivity that can change during execution. Progress in defect-free array assembly and programmable many-body systems has established the physical basis for arranging and controlling large registers [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] . Parallel Rydberg gates and multi-qubit experiments have advanced their computational capabilities [ 4 , 5 , 6 , 7 ] , while coherent transport enables entangled qubits to move between interaction configurations [ 8 ] . Logical processors and fault-tolerant architectural proposals further increase the importance of coordinating operations across these configurations [ 9 , 10 ] . Translating this flexibility into efficient execution depends on the compiler: unnecessary entangling pulses and atom transport consume time and coherence that could support useful computation. Quantum compilation has long addressed the gap between logical interactions and physical connectivity. Placement and allocation methods establish logical-to-physical assignments [ 11 , 12 ] ; heuristic routing, exact mapping, and scalable layout synthesis optimize the additional operations required by restricted connections [ 13 , 14 , 15 , 16 ] . Execution-time optimization and noise-adaptive mapping show that the appropriate objective also depends on operation durations and device characteristics [ 17 , 18 ] . Full-stack comparisons demonstrate the resulting interaction between architectural properties and compiler choices [ 19 ] . For neutral atoms, long-range interactions, topology displacement, and native multi-qubit operations introduce additional opportunities [ 20 , 21 , 22 ] . Recent compilers coordinate dynamic placement, parallel movement, and gate scheduling through constraint solving, decomposed optimization, and mobile ancillas [ 23 , 24 , 25 , 26 ] . Evaluating these methods requires benchmarks that expose the physical costs of their decisions. The first challenge is to establish an attainable performance reference for each workload. Application benchmarks provide important coverage: SupermarQ supplies scalable workloads and structural features [ 27 ] ; QASMBench collects low-level circuits and characterization metrics [ 28 ] ; and MQT Bench supplies consistent workloads across compilation abstraction levels [ 29 ] . On such workloads, observed differences show which compiler performs better under the tested conditions. Quantifying the remaining improvement opportunity additionally requires knowledge of what execution costs the circuit can attain. This need becomes particularly acute for neutral atoms, where fewer entangling stages can coexist with more transport. A reference must capture multiple physical resources and demonstrate that their combination is realizable. The second challenge is to diagnose the compiler decisions behind an observed resource gap. Excess movement may arise from initial placement, loss of reusable configurations, or overly fragmented routing batches, while additional entangling stages may result from limited parallelism or search that misses useful preparatory motion. Aggregate costs reveal the symptom but not its cause; controlled comparisons under the same circuit conditions are needed to isolate the responsible decision and determine whether improvement requires a better local objective or a richer search space. Constructive benchmarks address the reference problem by embedding solutions with known properties. QUEKO provides circuits with known optimal depth and gate counts and mappings requiring no inserted SWAPs [ 30 ] ; QKNOB embeds low-overhead transformations to evaluate SWAP and depth overhead [ 31 ] ; and QUBIKOS provides provably optimal nonzero SWAP costs and analyzes suboptimal routing decisions [ 32 ] . These frameworks target fixed coupling graphs, as found in superconducting processors. For neutral atoms, Khusainov et al. unify compiler-output representations and evaluation models for cross-toolchain comparison [ 33 ] , while Gao et al. develop linear and zigzag compilation strategies for the quantum Fourier transform (QFT), with analytical bounds on large atom movements [ 34 ] . Taken together, these efforts leave a need for a general framework that connects resource evaluation with compiler diagnosis under reconfigurable neutral-atom execution. Gate scheduling, atom placement, and parallel transport jointly determine physical execution costs, so a benchmark must provide not only an executable reference with jointly attainable targets for Rydberg stages, routing intervals, and movement layers, but also physical states that enable controlled investigation of the decisions behind resource gaps. Without these two capabilities, compiler outputs can be compared or individual resource bounds can be established, but systematically quantifying avoidable overhead across coupled resources and tracing it to specific compiler decisions remains difficult. We present NAKO, a benchmarking framework designed to address this need. NAKO constructs circuits parameterized by qubit count, logical depth, and requested one- and two-qubit gate densities, together with a target resource tuple ( R , T , M ) (R,T,M) . Each circuit is accompanied by an executable physical reference schedule that attains this tuple, with constructive guarantees of minimum Rydberg-stage and routing-interval counts and minimum movement among schedules with the minimum Rydberg-stage count. NAKO also provides a reference-guided workflow comprising resource comparison, controlled intervention, and execution validation. Its reference layouts support initial-mapping comparisons for identical circuits, while alternative gate and movement sequences are examined from the tested compiler’s own intermediate state. Figure 1 summarizes the framework, and Section III develops its construction, resource guarantees, and diagnostic workflow. Fig. 1: Overview of NAKO. Given workload and resource parameters, NAKO constructs a benchmark circuit C C , a certified resource target ( R , T , M ) (R,T,M) , and an executable physical witness S ref S_{\rm ref} . The compiler under test compiles C C ; NAKO compares the resulting schedule with the certified target to quantify resource gaps, and uses S ref S_{\rm ref} to diagnose the compiler decisions responsible for those gaps. The contributions are as follows. • Parameterized circuit construction. NAKO generates circuits with configurable qubit counts, depths, and gate densities, together with prescribed Rydberg-stage, routing-interval, and movement-layer targets. • Constructive optimality guarantees. An eight-qubit backbone and three composable primitives yield executable schedules and proofs of minimum Rydberg and routing counts, with minimum movement among minimum-Rydberg schedules. • Scalable generation. Direct construction produces 2000-qubit benchmarks in 4.97 s on average, enabling large-scale compiler testing. • Demonstrated compiler improvements. Evaluation across 648 runs guides targeted interventions in Enola and Optimal Layout Synthesis for Quantum Computing on dynamically field-programmable qubit arrays (OLSQ-DPQA), including a 78.9% reduction in Enola’s mean movement over five matched circuits.

sections.heading: II Background and Resource Metrics
sections.text: As discussed in Section I , comparing compiler outputs alone leaves unclear how much physical resource overhead is avoidable and which decisions cause it. For neutral atoms, resolving these questions requires accounting for both gate execution and the atom arrangements and movements that enable it. This section introduces the compilation process, its physical constraints, and the resource metrics used by NAKO. Figure 2 connects the constraints to the execution events counted by these metrics. sections.heading: II-A From Logical Gates to Physical Execution
sections.text: The input circuit specifies operations on Q Q qubits and their dependencies. Its logical depth D D counts dependency layers, while d 1 d_{1} and d 2 d_{2} describe the requested single- and two-qubit gate densities. A gate becomes ready when its predecessors have executed; disjoint ready gates are candidates for parallel execution. Throughout our compiler experiments, gates sharing a qubit retain their input order. Executing these candidates on neutral atoms requires an additional spatial decision. Each qubit is carried by an atom held in an optical trap. A spatial light modulator (SLM) supplies stationary traps, while acousto-optic deflectors (AODs) supply movable traps. AOD motion transports trapped atoms while preserving their quantum states. Transfers between aligned static and mobile traps change which atoms are carried by the AOD [ 8 , 23 , 26 ] . The compiler therefore selects a gate batch, arranges its atoms, and routes between successive arrangements. These choices produce a physical schedule containing gates, trap transfers, and movements. The constraints below determine which such schedules are feasible.

sections.heading: II-D Motivation for Benchmark Construction
sections.text: Gate scheduling, atom placement, and transport jointly determine the physical costs defined above. The resulting R R , T T , and M M values quantify resource use, but comparing these values across compilers leaves two questions unresolved: how much overhead is avoidable, and which decisions produce it. Answering the first requires resource targets that a valid schedule can attain under the coupled motion and global-pulse constraints. Answering the second requires controlled comparisons that connect the measured gap to specific compiler decisions. These requirements motivate constructing benchmark circuits together with their physical reference schedules. NAKO follows this approach to combine controllable workloads with attainable resource targets. Given a qubit count, logical depth, requested single- and two-qubit gate densities, and a feasible target tuple ( R , T , M ) (R,T,M) , NAKO produces a circuit in Quantum Assembly Language (QASM) and an executable schedule attaining that tuple. Under the dependency-preserving execution model considered here, R R and T T are minimal, and M M is minimal among executions with minimum R R . Direct construction also supports fast generation for parameter sweeps and large compiler tests. By pairing each circuit with known attainable resource targets, NAKO provides a concrete reference for quantifying resource gaps in compiler outputs. Its executable reference schedules also supply layouts and execution information for controlled tests of compiler decisions. Through this framework, we aim to identify avoidable overhead and guide targeted compiler improvements.

sections.heading: III-A Overview
sections.text: NAKO connects three stages: construction supplies a circuit and its physical reference; evaluation measures resource gaps and sensitivity; diagnosis tests the compilation decisions suggested by those measurements. The compiler under test receives the logical circuit and its hardware configuration. Resource targets and witness annotations remain available to the evaluation procedure, with initial mappings supplied explicitly in the paired mapping study. Figure 3 shows how NAKO constructs a circuit with the prescribed resources. It first builds an eight-qubit core, called the backbone, whose ordered CZ gates establish the resource bounds under the stated execution conditions. Small reusable construction blocks, called primitives, extend this core with known increments in ( R , T , M ) (R,T,M) ; the requested tuple determines how many instances of each primitive are needed. Additional gates, called filler gates, adjust circuit depth and gate load while preserving the resource targets. The required atom movements are recorded during construction, so the logical circuit and its physical reference schedule are produced together. Fig. 3: Construction with target ( R , T , M ) = ( 5 , 3 , 4 ) (R,T,M)=(5,3,4) . Initial matching, 111 111 , 223 223 , and 100 100 produce five pulses with movement counts 1 , 1 , 2 , 0 1,1,2,0 between them. Workload parameters determine the requested gate counts. In this example, subtracting the backbone’s 20 CZ gates from the request of 25 leaves five CZ gates to add; one static pair supplies these across the five pulses. The single-qubit request is completed with two Hadamard (H) gates. The resulting circuit contains 25 CZ gates and two H gates, and its reference retains ( R , T , M ) = ( 5 , 3 , 4 ) (R,T,M)=(5,3,4) . sections.heading: III-F From Resource Evaluation to Controlled Diagnosis
sections.text: NAKO pairs each generated circuit with attainable resource targets and an executable reference schedule. Building on these outputs, we design a reference-guided workflow for compiler evaluation and diagnosis, comprising resource comparison, controlled intervention, and execution validation. Resource comparison measures the tested compiler’s R R , T T , and M M against the targets for the same circuit. The resulting profile identifies the resources with excess cost. Inspection of the compiled schedule then guides the selection of a decision to investigate, such as initial placement, cross-stage layout reuse, or gate-batch selection. The intervention stage compares alternatives to the selected decision under matched conditions. To examine initial placement, the reference layout supplies an alternative mapping. Recompiling the same circuit with unchanged hardware and subsequent compiler settings measures the effect of this substitution. To examine a later scheduling or routing choice, we retain the executed operations and fix the compiler’s complete physical state, including atom positions and trap assignments. Alternative gate and movement sequences are then constructed from this common starting point. In the validation stage, the alternative executions are checked through the tested compiler’s instruction generator and physical replay, or by fixing candidate assignments in its constraint model. Checks cover gate identities and per-qubit order, physical feasibility, and resource costs. A validated cost reduction establishes an improvement opportunity under the stated controls. Section VI applies this workflow to Enola and OLSQ-DPQA.

sections.heading: IV Experimental Methodology
sections.text: The experiments assess NAKO’s ability to expose compiler resource overhead and support controlled diagnosis, together with the time and memory required to generate larger benchmarks.

sections.heading: IV-A Benchmarks and Evaluation Tasks
sections.text: All benchmark circuits are generated by NAKO with their resource targets and executable reference schedules. Experiments A, B, and C examine compiler responses to circuit depth, qubit count, and CZ load. Experiments D and E examine primitive compositions and feasible resource sweeps, while F supplies four eight-qubit constructions for investigating individual compilation decisions. CZ-load comparisons use achieved gate counts. Experiment G examines the diagnostic value of the reference initial layout by compiling the same five circuits under default initialization and the NAKO mapping. Experiment H separately measures the scalability of NAKO’s benchmark generation. Experiment I compiles five fixed circuits across four hardware grids to examine resource use and completion under different capacities. Table III summarizes the experimental design. sections.heading: IV-B Compilers and Experimental Settings
sections.text: The evaluation uses Enola [ 26 ] and OLSQ-DPQA [ 23 ] , two neutral-atom compilers with different compilation approaches. Enola separates gate scheduling, atom placement, and routing in a heuristic pipeline. OLSQ-DPQA uses SMT-based layout and movement synthesis. These approaches provide complementary settings for examining the resource gaps and compiler decisions that NAKO can reveal. Compiler experiments use the CZ portion of each generated circuit, retaining all qubits and the gate order on each qubit. This preserves the dependency condition used in NAKO’s resource guarantees. Enola uses routing based on maximal independent sets and dynamic layout updates between Rydberg stages; OLSQ-DPQA uses its greedy compilation mode with gate commutation disabled. In G, only the initial mapping changes between the paired runs; subsequent compiler settings remain fixed. Outside I, both compilers use 16 × 16 16\times 16 spatial grids with 16 AOD rows and columns. In I, an r × c r\times c logical site grid is represented by a 2 ​ c × r 2c\times r spatial grid in Enola and a c × r c\times r grid in OLSQ-DPQA, with corresponding AOD dimensions. These configurations follow the compilers’ respective representations of the two-slot site model. Each compilation has a time limit of 10 000 s, with up to eight compilations running concurrently per compiler. Compiler experiments run on Linux with Python 3.10.19; OLSQ-DPQA uses Z3 5.1.0. Generation scalability is measured separately on Windows with Python 3.12.14 and a fixed 64 × 64 64\times 64 site grid. Timing includes circuit construction, serialization, and QASM reload and statistics collection. Memory measurements report peak traced Python allocations.

sections.heading: V Evaluation Results
sections.text: The experiments compare compiler resource costs with NAKO’s attainable targets and examine how the resulting gaps depend on workload size, interaction structure, initial placement, and hardware capacity. These comparisons guide the controlled investigations in Section VI . Generation time and memory are measured separately to assess the cost of producing larger benchmarks.

sections.heading: V-E Small Primitive Compositions
sections.text: Experiment F tests whether resource gaps already arise in small, directly inspectable primitive constructions. sections.heading: V-F Reference Initial Mappings
sections.text: Experiment G examines how initial placement affects the measured resource gaps. Each of five circuits, with reference ( 16 , 12 , 18 ) (16,12,18) , is compiled using its default mapping and the initial mapping from its NAKO reference. sections.heading: VI Reference-Guided Compiler Diagnosis
sections.text: The NAKO evaluation reveals different resource gaps in the two compilers. Enola attains the reference R R throughout the main workloads, while its mean movement ratio is approximately 37. OLSQ-DPQA exceeds the reference R R and T T on the small primitive constructions and exhibits capacity-dependent completion on the hardware sweep. We trace these observations through controlled comparisons of compiler decisions, using reference layouts, small benchmark constructions, and validated alternative executions.

sections.heading: VI-A Enola: Locating and Prioritizing Movement Losses
sections.text: The movement gap persists across NAKO’s depth, width, and interaction-load experiments. Experiment G further shows that supplying the reference initial layout reduces Enola’s movement while preserving its R R and T T . Figure 13 follows this observed placement sensitivity through cross-stage layout controls, placement-score comparisons, and gathering-batch tests. Fig. 13: NAKO’s diagnostic workflow for Enola. Numbered process steps progress from resource evaluation through controlled placement and layout probes to attribution and repair priorities. The lower objects summarize findings produced by each step. Detailed interventions and measurements appear in the text and tables.

sections.heading: VI-A 1 Reference evaluation and placement probe
sections.text: The five G circuits each contain 128 CZ gates and have reference ( 16 , 12 , 18 ) (16,12,18) . Replacing Enola’s default initial layout with the NAKO layout reduces mean M M from 758.8 to 553, with R = 16 R=16 and T = 15 T=15 in both modes. Enola subsequently updates atom placement between stages and gathers gate pairs in batches of operations compatible with the AOD constraints. To examine how the supplied layout affects the full execution, we compare dynamic updates with repeated use of the initial configuration.

sections.heading: VI-A 2 Cross-stage layout management
sections.text: Enola’s return-to-initial-layout option restores the initial atom positions after each Rydberg stage, giving successive stages the same starting layout. We apply both dynamic and return policies to the default and NAKO layouts. The scheduled CZ layers, hardware, router, and instruction generator remain fixed. Table VI reports the resulting costs. Layout Boundary policy Mean M M Fidelity Default Dynamic 758.8 0.171 Default Return 777.2 0.167 NAKO Dynamic 553.0 0.188 NAKO Return 160.0 0.235 With the NAKO layout, returning after each stage reduces mean M M from 553 to 160, approximately 71.1%. With the default layout, the same policy increases M M from 758.8 to 777.2. The effect of preserving a configuration therefore depends on its layout. Repeated use of the NAKO configuration provides a substantially cheaper execution under Enola’s own router, while dynamic updates increase the movement generated from that same initial layout. The default configuration remains expensive under both policies. These results identify a strong dependence between layout choice and the cost of cross-stage updates.

sections.heading: VI-A 3 Placement objective and execution cost
sections.text: The fixed-boundary executions produce a large cost difference between the two layout families: mean M M is 777.2 for the default layouts and 160 for the NAKO layouts. To examine how the compiler evaluates these configurations, we compute its placement objective on both. The objective minimizes a weighted sum of gate-endpoint distances over upcoming CZ layers. It assigns approximately 54.6 to the default layouts and 75.6 to the NAKO layouts, ranking the more expensive executions ahead of the cheaper ones. This ranking reversal on the NAKO inputs leads to an independent check using a single four-CZ matching. One layout scores 9.37 and produces 16 movement layers with a modeled duration of about 1.00 ms; another scores 9.82 and produces 14 movement layers with a duration of about 0.75 ms. Each layout uses its minimum gathering-batch count. The lower-distance layout remains more expensive after batch-count optimization within each layout. Gate-endpoint distance evaluates pairs individually, while physical execution also depends on compatible gathering operations and their loading and unloading sequence. The two comparisons expose a concrete mismatch between the placement proxy’s ordering and the costs of executable plans.

sections.heading: VI-A 4 Routing batches and repair priorities
sections.text: On the same five NAKO inputs with fixed stage boundaries, Enola’s original selector uses averages of 34 gathering batches for the default layouts and 20 for the NAKO layouts. To measure the contribution of batch selection, we compare its maximal-independent-set heuristic with enumeration of the minimum batch count for each layout. Enumeration considers both gathering directions of each gate under the original compatibility test. Both selectors use the same router and instruction generator. Table VII summarizes the results. TABLE VII: Enola batching controls with fixed stage boundaries. Minimum batches refers to the number of gathering batches. Layout Selector Mean batches Mean M M Default Original 34.0 777.2 Default Minimum batches 32.8 754.4 NAKO Original 20.0 160.0 NAKO Minimum batches 20.0 160.0 For the default layouts, enumeration reduces mean batch count from 34 to 32.8 and mean M M from 777.2 to 754.4. Mean modeled fidelity improves by approximately 1.8%; the strongest sample removes three batches and reduces movement by 8.2%. For the NAKO layouts, both selectors produce 20 batches and M = 160 M=160 . Batch selection therefore provides additional savings for the default configurations, while the preserved NAKO configurations already attain the minimum batch count. The controlled executions preserve the scheduled CZ layers and pass physical replay of trap activation, coordinate updates, global-pulse gate pairs, and final states. Additional quantum-volume (QV) and QFT matching-slice tests use 40 preset layouts each. Enumeration removes excess gathering batches in nine QV layouts and improves movement and modeled fidelity in each. The original selector attains the minimum batch count in all 40 tested QFT layouts. The movement gap measured against NAKO’s targets is traced to placement-score mismatch and costly updates of the reference layout. Reusing that layout reduces mean M M from 553 to 160 through Enola’s own router and instruction generator, while minimum-batch selection provides smaller, layout-dependent gains (Tables VI and VII ). NAKO supplies both the attainable resource target that directs the investigation and the executable layout used to test compiler choices. These controls yield validated movement reductions and establish layout selection and cross-stage reuse as the primary improvement priorities for the five inputs.

sections.heading: VI-B OLSQ-DPQA: Connecting Quality and Reliability
sections.text: NAKO’s four small primitive constructions exhibit excess Rydberg stages and routing intervals even at eight qubits. The hardware-capacity experiment additionally shows declining completion on tighter grids for unchanged circuits. Figure 14 develops these observations into two investigations: the cost of accepted gate batches and the progression of local search after failure. Fig. 14: NAKO’s diagnostic workflow for OLSQ-DPQA. sections.heading: VI-B 1 Quality branch: fixed-state alternatives
sections.text: The one- 223 223 input in experiment F contains eight qubits and twelve CZ gates arranged in three distinct successive matchings. Its NAKO reference is ( 3 , 2 , 3 ) (3,2,3) , while OLSQ-DPQA produces ( 5 , 4 , 4 ) (5,4,4) . To examine where the additional pulses arise, we trace its gate-batch decisions and select the state after the third pulse, where four CZ gates remain ready for execution. We retain the complete executed prefix and fix atom coordinates, trap assignments, and AOD row and column identifiers at this checkpoint. These variables preserve the physical starting conditions and shared-motion groups for the subsequent operations. OLSQ-DPQA selects a batch through a local constraint query whose horizon specifies the number of modeled state transitions. From this state, one-step queries are unsatisfiable when required to execute four or three gates and satisfiable for two gates. The controller accepts the two-gate batch and executes the remaining two gates after another movement. Its suffix places a pulse after each of two movement layers. A candidate generated under the same physical constraints uses the first movement to prepare the geometry and the second to bring all four gate pairs together for one pulse. Both suffixes use two movement layers, while the preparatory candidate combines them into one routing interval before a single Rydberg stage. The complete program consequently changes from ( 5 , 4 , 4 ) (5,4,4) to ( 4 , 3 , 4 ) (4,3,4) . The resource reduction is obtained with the circuit, prefix, complete physical state, hardware, and movement budget fixed. Inspection of the controller explains the observed choice: it decreases the required gate count within the one-step query and accepts the first feasible bound. It advances to a two-step horizon after every positive one-step bound fails. sections.heading: VI-B 2 Reliability branch: preparation and progress
sections.text: Experiment I compiles the same five NAKO circuits across progressively tighter grids. OLSQ-DPQA completes all five on the widest grid and times out on all five on the two tightest grids. Examining the 12 timeout traces reveals thousands of repeated local failures after the last compilation progress. The controller repeatedly returns to a two-step query. Its source resets the horizon to two whenever the gate bound reaches zero, reproducing that search horizon at the unchanged execution state. The dependence on hardware capacity directs the analysis to the query’s site-occupancy constraints. Its interaction-exactness condition applies at every modeled state after the initial checkpoint: co-located atom pairs must execute gates at that state. For a matching of ready gates, G s G_{s} executed gates pair 2 ​ G s 2G_{s} atoms, while the remaining atoms occupy individual sites. A state with N N atoms therefore occupies at least N − G s N-G_{s} sites. With S S available sites, G s ≥ max ⁡ ( 0 , N − S ) . G_{s}\geq\max(0,N-S). (13) Across k k encoded states, each ready gate is executed once, so the query requires at least k ​ max ⁡ ( 0 , N − S ) k\max(0,N-S) ready gates. At the 2 × 8 2\times 8 checkpoint of sample I-4, 20 atoms share 16 sites and six gates are ready. Each encoded state requires at least four gates, giving a requirement of eight across the two-state query. This exceeds the available six gates and explains the query’s unsatisfiability at that checkpoint. To examine state representation and search horizon separately, we construct a four-qubit, one-CZ control with a fixed initial physical state. The queries vary hardware width, horizon, and the condition under which interaction exactness applies. In the pulse-guarded model, exactness applies when a Rydberg pulse is active; movement-only states can retain co-located atoms while preparing subsequent gates. The AOD motion, transfer, ordering, and crowding constraints are retained. Table IX reports the query outcomes. TABLE IX: OLSQ-DPQA preparation-state controls. Preparation in this control therefore depends on both the admitted intermediate states and the explored horizon. The feasible three-step execution identifies the longer horizon needed to progress from that same state.

sections.heading: VI-B 3 A unified design direction
sections.text: The quality and reliability results identify three linked decisions: accepting a gate batch, representing preparation states, and advancing search after failure. The resulting design priorities are to compare immediate and preparatory candidates by incremental R R , T T , and M M , apply interaction exactness under explicit pulse activation, and expand the horizon after a failed state–horizon query. Across the four NAKO constructions, validated suffix replacements save one Rydberg stage and one routing interval at unchanged movement (Table VIII ). These improvements are obtained from the compiler’s own checkpoints and locate a recoverable part of the R / T R/T gap in its batch-acceptance rule. The compact-hardware controls additionally identify preparation-state encoding and horizon progression as causes of local search failure (Table IX ). NAKO’s attainable targets reveal the resource excess, and its small circuit families support the fixed-state comparisons that turn that observation into lower-cost executions and specific compiler design changes.

sections.heading: VII Conclusion
sections.text: NAKO evaluates neutral-atom compilers through parameterized circuits with attainable R, T, and M targets and executable reference schedules. Under dependency-preserving execution, its backbone and composable primitives establish minimum R and T, with M minimal among schedules attaining minimum R. Comparisons with these references quantify compiler resource gaps, while the benchmark families support systematic evaluation of workload sensitivity. Direct construction also makes large-scale testing practical, producing 2000-qubit benchmarks in about five seconds. The observed resource gaps guide controlled investigations of compiler decisions. Reference-layout comparisons expose placement-score mismatch and costly cross-stage updates in Enola; validated interventions reduce mean M by 78.9% on five matched circuits. The OLSQ-DPQA study links extra stages to batch acceptance and local search failures to preparation-state representation and horizon progression. Four validated suffix replacements each save one Rydberg stage and one routing interval at unchanged movement. These cases show how NAKO’s attainable targets and physical references connect measured resource overhead to specific compiler decisions and verified execution improvements.

Abstract Reconfigurable neutral-atom processors couple gate scheduling, atom placement, and parallel atom transport, so compiler decisions jointly determine physical execution costs. Evaluating these compilers requires attainable resource references and a way to trace excess costs to their causes. We present NAKO, a benchmarking framework that parameterizes circuits by qubit count, logical depth, and requested one- and two-qubit gate densities, and assigns attainable targets for Rydberg stages, routing intervals, and movement layers. Each benchmark is paired with an executable reference schedule; under the stated execution model, construction guarantees minimum Rydberg-stage and routing-interval counts, and minimum movement among schedules with the minimum Rydberg-stage count. Comparing compiler outputs with these references quantifies resource gaps, while reference mappings and intermediate physical states enable controlled interventions that trace excess costs to specific compiler decisions. In a 648-run evaluation of Enola and OLSQ-DPQA, NAKO identifies distinct bottlenecks. For Enola, placement scoring and cross-stage layout management contribute to excess movement; diagnosis-guided interventions reduce mean movement by 78.9% across five matched circuits. For OLSQ-DPQA, premature candidate selection and limited exploration of preparatory states produce avoidable entangling stages and routing intervals; four fixed-checkpoint continuations each eliminate one Rydberg stage and one routing interval without increasing movement. NAKO thus links resource targets backed by constructive optimality guarantees to controlled diagnosis and validation of compiler-specific resource savings. Index Terms: Neutral-atom quantum computing, compiler evaluation, benchmark generation, layout synthesis, atom routing, compiler diagnosis. I Introduction Reconfigurable neutral-atom processors combine scalable atomic arrays with connectivity that can change during execution. Progress in defect-free array assembly and programmable many-body systems has established the physical basis for arranging and controlling large registers [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] . Parallel Rydberg gates and multi-qubit experiments have advanced their computational capabilities [ 4 , 5 , 6 , 7 ] , while coherent transport enables entangled qubits to move between interaction configurations [ 8 ] . Logical processors and fault-tolerant architectural proposals further increase the importance of coordinating operations across these configurations [ 9 , 10 ] . Translating this flexibility into efficient execution depends on the compiler: unnecessary entangling pulses and atom transport consume time and coherence that could support useful computation. Quantum compilation has long addressed the gap between logical interactions and physical connectivity. Placement and allocation methods establish logical-to-physical assignments [ 11 , 12 ] ; heuristic routing, exact mapping, and scalable layout synthesis optimize the additional operations required by restricted connections [ 13 , 14 , 15 , 16 ] . Execution-time optimization and noise-adaptive mapping show that the appropriate objective also depends on operation durations and device characteristics [ 17 , 18 ] . Full-stack comparisons demonstrate the resulting interaction between architectural properties and compiler choices [ 19 ] . For neutral atoms, long-range interactions, topology displacement, and native multi-qubit operations introduce additional opportunities [ 20 , 21 , 22 ] . Recent compilers coordinate dynamic placement, parallel movement, and gate scheduling through constraint solving, decomposed optimization, and mobile ancillas [ 23 , 24 , 25 , 26 ] . Evaluating these methods requires benchmarks that expose the physical costs of their decisions. The first challenge is to establish an attainable performance reference for each workload. Application benchmarks provide important coverage: SupermarQ supplies scalable workloads and structural features [ 27 ] ; QASMBench collects low-level circuits and characterization metrics [ 28 ] ; and MQT Bench supplies consistent workloads across compilation abstraction levels [ 29 ] . On such workloads, observed differences show which compiler performs better under the tested conditions. Quantifying the remaining improvement opportunity additionally requires knowledge of what execution costs the circuit can attain. This need becomes particularly acute for neutral atoms, where fewer entangling stages can coexist with more transport. A reference must capture multiple physical resources and demonstrate that their combination is realizable. The second challenge is to diagnose the compiler decisions behind an observed resource gap. Excess movement may arise from initial placement, loss of reusable configurations, or overly fragmented routing batches, while additional entangling stages may result from limited parallelism or search that misses useful preparatory motion. Aggregate costs reveal the symptom but not its cause; controlled comparisons under the same circuit conditions are needed to isolate the responsible decision and determine whether improvement requires a better local objective or a richer search space. Constructive benchmarks address the reference problem by embedding solutions with known properties. QUEKO provides circuits with known optimal depth and gate counts and mappings requiring no inserted SWAPs [ 30 ] ; QKNOB embeds low-overhead transformations to evaluate SWAP and depth overhead [ 31 ] ; and QUBIKOS provides provably optimal nonzero SWAP costs and analyzes suboptimal routing decisions [ 32 ] . These frameworks target fixed coupling graphs, as found in superconducting processors. For neutral atoms, Khusainov et al. unify compiler-output representations and evaluation models for cross-toolchain comparison [ 33 ] , while Gao et al. develop linear and zigzag compilation strategies for the quantum Fourier transform (QFT), with analytical bounds on large atom movements [ 34 ] . Taken together, these efforts leave a need for a general framework that connects resource evaluation with compiler diagnosis under reconfigurable neutral-atom execution. Gate scheduling, atom placement, and parallel transport jointly determine physical execution costs, so a benchmark must provide not only an executable reference with jointly attainable targets for Rydberg stages, routing intervals, and movement layers, but also physical states that enable controlled investigation of the decisions behind resource gaps. Without these two capabilities, compiler outputs can be compared or individual resource bounds can be established, but systematically quantifying avoidable overhead across coupled resources and tracing it to specific compiler decisions remains difficult. We present NAKO, a benchmarking framework designed to address this need. NAKO constructs circuits parameterized by qubit count, logical depth, and requested one- and two-qubit gate densities, together with a target resource tuple ( R , T , M ) (R,T,M) . Each circuit is accompanied by an executable physical reference schedule that attains this tuple, with constructive guarantees of minimum Rydberg-stage and routing-interval counts and minimum movement among schedules with the minimum Rydberg-stage count. NAKO also provides a reference-guided workflow comprising resource comparison, controlled intervention, and execution validation. Its reference layouts support initial-mapping comparisons for identical circuits, while alternative gate and movement sequences are examined from the tested compiler’s own intermediate state. Given workload and resource parameters, NAKO constructs a benchmark circuit C C , a certified resource target ( R , T , M ) (R,T,M) , and an executable physical witness S ref S_{\rm ref} . The compiler under test compiles C C ; NAKO compares the resulting schedule with the certified target to quantify resource gaps, and uses S ref S_{\rm ref} to diagnose the compiler decisions responsible for those gaps. The contributions are as follows. • Parameterized circuit construction. NAKO generates circuits with configurable qubit counts, depths, and gate densities, together with prescribed Rydberg-stage, routing-interval, and movement-layer targets. • Constructive optimality guarantees. An eight-qubit backbone and three composable primitives yield executable schedules and proofs of minimum Rydberg and routing counts, with minimum movement among minimum-Rydberg schedules. • Scalable generation. Direct construction produces 2000-qubit benchmarks in 4.97 s on average, enabling large-scale compiler testing. • Demonstrated compiler improvements. Evaluation across 648 runs guides targeted interventions in Enola and Optimal Layout Synthesis for Quantum Computing on dynamically field-programmable qubit arrays (OLSQ-DPQA), including a 78.9% reduction in Enola’s mean movement over five matched circuits. II-D Motivation for Benchmark Construction Gate scheduling, atom placement, and transport jointly determine the physical costs defined above. The resulting R R , T T , and M M values quantify resource use, but comparing these values across compilers leaves two questions unresolved: how much overhead is avoidable, and which decisions produce it. Answering the first requires resource targets that a valid schedule can attain under the coupled motion and global-pulse constraints. Answering the second requires controlled comparisons that connect the measured gap to specific compiler decisions. These requirements motivate constructing benchmark circuits together with their physical reference schedules. NAKO follows this approach to combine controllable workloads with attainable resource targets. Given a qubit count, logical depth, requested single- and two-qubit gate densities, and a feasible target tuple ( R , T , M ) (R,T,M) , NAKO produces a circuit in Quantum Assembly Language (QASM) and an executable schedule attaining that tuple. Under the dependency-preserving execution model considered here, R R and T T are minimal, and M M is minimal among executions with minimum R R . Direct construction also supports fast generation for parameter sweeps and large compiler tests. By pairing each circuit with known attainable resource targets, NAKO provides a concrete reference for quantifying resource gaps in compiler outputs. Its executable reference schedules also supply layouts and execution information for controlled tests of compiler decisions. Through this framework, we aim to identify avoidable overhead and guide targeted compiler improvements. III-F From Resource Evaluation to Controlled Diagnosis NAKO pairs each generated circuit with attainable resource targets and an executable reference schedule. Building on these outputs, we design a reference-guided workflow for compiler evaluation and diagnosis, comprising resource comparison, controlled intervention, and execution validation. Resource comparison measures the tested compiler’s R R , T T , and M M against the targets for the same circuit. The resulting profile identifies the resources with excess cost. Inspection of the compiled schedule then guides the selection of a decision to investigate, such as initial placement, cross-stage layout reuse, or gate-batch selection. The intervention stage compares alternatives to the selected decision under matched conditions. To examine initial placement, the reference layout supplies an alternative mapping. Recompiling the same circuit with unchanged hardware and subsequent compiler settings measures the effect of this substitution. To examine a later scheduling or routing choice, we retain the executed operations and fix the compiler’s complete physical state, including atom positions and trap assignments. Alternative gate and movement sequences are then constructed from this common starting point. In the validation stage, the alternative executions are checked through the tested compiler’s instruction generator and physical replay, or by fixing candidate assignments in its constraint model. Checks cover gate identities and per-qubit order, physical feasibility, and resource costs. A validated cost reduction establishes an improvement opportunity under the stated controls.
